title: mock-theta-census: a numerical census of Ramanujan-style q-series and the sign-twisted fifth-order functions ψ₀*, ψ₁*
description:
A computational search for Ramanujan-style mock theta functions. A classifier based on radial asymptotics at 19 roots of unity (Arb ball arithmetic) sorts q-series into modular, mock, quantum-type and neither, and classifies the known functions of a 51-function validation catalog correctly (the one exception, a sum of two modular forms with different offsets, is a documented limitation). A census of 8,869 distinct Eulerian series finds 25 mock theta functions, all identified: 23 are known functions, rescalings or specializations of the universal mock theta function g₂, and two are half a fifth-order function plus half of a sign-twisted companion.

The companions ψ₁*(q) = Σ (−1)ⁿ q^{n(n+1)/2} (−q;q)ₙ and ψ₀*(q) = Σ (−1)ⁿ q^{(n+1)(n+2)/2} (−q;q)ₙ satisfy 2ψ₀* = f₀* − θ₄·R₀ and 2ψ₁* = f₁* + θ₄·R₁, with R₀, R₁ the entire Rogers–Ramanujan function at a = 1, q (OEIS A039924, A224898). Their expansion at q = −1 has integer coefficients whose large-order behaviour is governed by R₀, R₁ (constants in ℚ(√5)); radial limits at odd-order roots appear to equal one third of the first period (numerical). Proof status of every claim is marked in the documents.

Version 1.2 adds sign twists of all catalog mock theta functions (bounded, non-trivial companions also for the fifth-order F₀, F₁, the third-order ψ and the eighth-order T₀) and a rank-2 census of 6,327 double sums. Its one mock candidate, D(q) = Σ q^{m²−mn+n²}/((−q;q)ₘ(−q;q)ₙ), has the growth fingerprint of the third-order f(q). At q = 1 its exact expansion has the golden-ratio large-order constants found for ψ* at q = −1: π²/60, π·K² = 8(5+√5)/25, s₁ = (35+6√5)/300 (numerical).

Includes code, data, a formula sheet in several notations, a rank-2 (double-sum) census pipeline, and interactive pages (https://quasimondo.github.io/mock-theta-census/). Code: MIT. Data and documents: CC BY 4.0.

Made by Mario Klingemann with extensive assistance from AI models (Anthropic's Claude), which wrote most of the code and analysis under his direction; see the README section 'How this was made'.
